books.title: Taste This
books.art_why: All the foods shown are real everyday foods that can be photographed today.

pages.text: Introduction We use our tongue to taste. Foods can taste salty, bitter, sour, or sweet.
pages.brief: An extreme close-up of an open mouth with the tongue pushed out and slightly curled, photographed from the front in soft daylight. The tongue fills most of the frame so its rough surface is clear, with lips and chin at the edges.

pages.text: Can you guess how these foods can taste?
pages.brief: A plain table photographed from above, holding a small spread of different foods on separate little plates, colours and textures contrasting: crisp, soft, glossy, dull. A fork rests beside them and daylight falls evenly across the surface.

pages.text: Salty Taste These are pretzels. Pretzels can taste salty. We use salt to give foods a salty flavor.
pages.brief: A bowl piled with twisted pretzels, photographed close so the shiny brown crusts and coarse white salt grains show clearly. A small dish of loose salt sits beside the bowl on a plain wooden table, light catching the crystals.

pages.text: Bitter Taste This is spinach. Spinach can taste bitter. Some people do not like bitter flavors.
pages.brief: A bunch of fresh spinach leaves, dark green and glossy, heaped on a plain pale surface, photographed close so the veins and crinkled edges are visible. A few loose leaves lie scattered beside the bunch in soft even light.

pages.text: Sour and Sweet Taste This is a lemon. Lemons can taste sour. Some people do not like sour flavors.
pages.brief: A whole lemon and one lemon cut in half, the cut face turned to the camera so the juicy segments and pale pith show. Both sit on a plain light surface with a drop of juice beside them and bright daylight from the side.

pages.text: This is honey. Honey can taste sweet. We use honey to give foods a sweet flavor.
pages.brief: A glass jar of golden honey with a wooden dipper lifted out, a thick thread of honey running back down into the jar. The jar stands on a plain pale table, backlit so the honey glows amber.

pages.text: These are apples. Apples can taste sweet or sour. Do you like sweet apples? Or do you like sour apples?
pages.brief: Several apples on a plain surface, some deep red and some bright green, one cut open to show pale flesh and seeds. They sit in a loose row, photographed close in soft daylight so the shiny skins stand out.

pages.text: Conclusion How do your favorite foods taste? fruit cheeseburger nuts chocolate.
pages.brief: A table spread photographed from above: chocolate chip cookies, pieces of sushi, fresh fruit, a cheeseburger, shelled nuts and a bar of chocolate, each on its own small plate. Daylight falls evenly so every food is sharp.

pages.text: Brussels sprouts grapefruit juice potato chips popcorn.
pages.brief: A wide arrangement on a pale table: a ripe tomato, a kiwi cut in half, a bowl of cereal, small Brussels sprouts, a glass of grapefruit juice, a bowl of potato chips and a bowl of popcorn, photographed close together in bright daylight.

books.title: Firefighters
books.art_why: Firefighters, trucks, ladders and planes all exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Have you ever heard a fire truck racing to a fire? The truck is full of firefighters. Firefighters help keep us safe.
pages.brief: A bright red fire truck races down a city street with lights flashing, seen from the side. Inside the cab, firefighters in helmets sit ready. Behind them the truck is packed with gear. The street is busy with a road and buildings, showing the truck on its way to a fire.

pages.text: Firefighters fight many kinds of fires.
pages.brief: Firefighters in full gear work at different kinds of fires. One group sprays at flames coming from a building, another stands near burning grass in an open field. Smoke rises around them, and the firefighters wear helmets, thick coats and boots as they face the flames.

pages.text: Firefighters use many tools. Firefighters use ladders to reach high places. Firefighters help keep us safe.
pages.brief: A firefighter climbs a tall metal ladder that reaches high up the side of a building. The ladder is raised from a fire truck parked below. The firefighter wears a helmet and heavy protective clothing, holding on carefully while looking up toward a high window.

pages.text: Firefighters use hoses to spray water. Firefighters help keep us safe.
pages.brief: Two firefighters stand side by side holding a thick hose, spraying a strong stream of water forward. Water arches through the air toward a smoking doorway. Both wear helmets, heavy coats and gloves, and their boots are planted firmly on the ground as they work.

pages.text: Firefighters use axes to break down doors. They use masks to breathe safely.
pages.brief: A firefighter swings an axe to break down a wooden door, chips of wood flying. Beside them another firefighter wears a face mask over the nose and mouth to breathe safely, with an air tank on the back. Both wear helmets and thick protective coats in the smoke.

pages.text: Firefighters use machines. They use trucks and boats to spray water on fires. They use planes and helicopters to dump water on forest fires.
pages.brief: Firefighting machines at work: a fire truck and a fire boat spray water, while a plane and a helicopter fly low over a forest fire, dumping water from above. Smoke rises from the trees below, and the boats sit on open water near the shore.

pages.text: Firefighters are strong. They help keep us safe.
pages.brief: Strong firefighters in helmets and heavy coats carry equipment and stand steady together. One lifts a heavy hose, another holds a tool, their arms and shoulders showing effort. They stand close to their fire truck, ready to help, calm and solid in their gear.

pages.text: Firefighters go to school. They learn to fight fires. They learn to keep people safe.
pages.brief: Firefighter students sit in a training classroom, watching an instructor. Charts and equipment are around the room, and the students wear uniforms. Later they practise outdoors with hoses and ladders, learning how to fight fires and how to keep people safe.

pages.text: Firefighters help keep fires from starting. They teach other people about fires, too.
pages.brief: A firefighter stands in front of a small group of people, talking and pointing to a display about fire safety. The grown-ups and children listen closely. Nearby, a firefighter checks a smoke alarm and clears dry grass away from a building to help stop fires from starting.

pages.text: Firefighters help people and save lives. Firefighters help keep us safe.
pages.brief: A firefighter kneels down to help a frightened child, speaking gently, while another firefighter guides an older person to safety away from a smoking building. The firefighters wear helmets and heavy coats, and their truck waits nearby as people are led to a safe place.

books.title: Smart Crows
books.art_why: Crows are real animals that can be photographed.

pages.text: Crows are smart. They are as smart as elephants. They are as smart as apes.
pages.brief: A glossy black crow stands on a branch in a natural outdoor setting, looking alert. Nearby, a large elephant and a group of apes are shown in their own surroundings, placing the crow beside these clever animals in a simple comparison of intelligence.

pages.text: Crows solve problems. Crows use tools.
pages.brief: One crow works at a simple problem in a natural outdoor setting, using a small tool held in its beak. Another crow nearby watches the first crow, showing crows solving problems and using tools as they work.

pages.text: Crows build nests from things we throw away.
pages.brief: Crows build a nest in a tree using discarded things people throw away. Bits of scraps and cast-off material are woven into the nest, while the crows work together in an outdoor setting to shape their home from what others have left behind.

pages.text: Crows let cars crack nuts for them. Crows drop nuts on the road. Cars drive over the nuts. When the light turns red, crows hop out and fetch their snack!
pages.brief: Crows drop nuts onto a road where cars drive over them and crack the shells. When the traffic light turns red, the crows hop out onto the road and fetch their snack, showing how they let cars crack nuts for them.

pages.text: Hey, it’s Joe! So it is. Hey Joe, what do you know? Crows learn human faces. They can pick out those faces in a crowd.
pages.brief: A crow perches above a crowd of people, its head turned as it studies the many human faces below. One familiar face in the crowd stands out to the crow, showing how crows learn human faces and can pick them out in a crowd.

pages.text: Use your indoor voice, please. Crows use soft calls with family members. Crows use louder calls with other crows.
pages.brief: A family group of crows sits close together in a tree, their beaks slightly open in soft calls. Farther away, other crows call more loudly across an open outdoor space, showing the different calls crows use with family members and with other crows.

pages.text: Crows work together to find food. They work together to protect their family.
pages.brief: A group of crows works together on the ground, searching for food as a team. Nearby, other crows stay close around a family group, showing how crows cooperate to find food and to protect their family in the wild.

pages.text: Do I know you? Nope. I’m just here to help. Crows even defend crows they don’t know.
pages.brief: One crow steps forward to help an unfamiliar crow, standing close in a protective pose outdoors. The two crows face the same direction together, showing that crows will defend even crows they do not know and are not part of their family.

pages.text: Crows gather to say good-bye to dead crows.
pages.brief: A group of crows gathers quietly on the ground around a dead crow, standing close together in an outdoor setting. Their still, attentive poses show the gathering as a good-bye to the dead crow, with the crows staying near one another.

pages.text: Crows watch and learn and feel, like us. Crows are smart, like you.
pages.brief: A crow perches alertly on a branch, watching a natural outdoor scene with bright, attentive eyes. Its calm, expressive posture suggests it is learning and feeling, showing the crow as a smart animal that watches, learns and feels, much like a child.

books.title: Night Animals
books.art_why: Real night animals and their behaviour exist today, so photographs fit.

pages.text: Introduction Some animals are active at night, when it is dark. These animals sleep during the day while the Sun shines.
pages.brief: A dark night scene with several animals awake and moving through the shadows, wide eyes and alert bodies. Beside it, the same kinds of animals sleep curled up while bright sunlight shines over the daytime scene.

pages.text: These animals have special eyes to help them see in the dark. Most of them also hear and smell well. Their senses help them find food at night.
pages.brief: Close view of an animal's large shining eyes in the dark, with ears pricked and nose lifted, sniffing and listening. Around it, dim shapes of nighttime animals use their senses to search for food in the darkness.

pages.text: In the Air This owl is active at night. It catches mice and rats in the dark.
pages.brief: An owl swoops low through the dark night sky, wings spread wide, sharp eyes fixed downward. Below, a mouse and a rat scurry over the ground as the owl's talons reach for them.

pages.text: This bat is active at night. It eats fruit and nectar in the dark.
pages.brief: A bat flies through the dark night, wings stretched out, nibbling a piece of fruit and dipping toward a flower for nectar. Fruit and blossoms surround it in the shadows.

pages.text: In Water This nurse shark is active at night. It finds crabs and clams in the dark.
pages.brief: A nurse shark glides low over the sandy seafloor in dark night water, its mouth near crabs and clams scattered on the bottom. Murky blue darkness surrounds the shark and its prey.

pages.text: This hermit crab is active at night. It looks for little fish and worms in the dark.
pages.brief: A hermit crab carries its shell across the dark seafloor at night, claws reaching toward little fish and worms nearby. Small fish swim and worms lie in the sand around the crab.

pages.text: On Land This tiger is active at night. It hunts deer and wild pigs in the dark.
pages.brief: A tiger stalks through dark night grass, eyes glowing, body low and ready. Ahead, a deer and wild pigs stand in the shadows as the tiger hunts them.

pages.text: Are you active at night or during the day?
pages.brief: A young child lies awake in bed at night with eyes wide open, looking into the dark room. In a second scene, the same child is outside, running and playing actively in bright sunshine during the day.

books.title: Are You From India?
books.art_why: All the animals and places exist in the real world today, so photographs suit the book.

pages.text: I am from a country called India. Many animals live here.
pages.brief: A young Indian child stands in a bright green landscape with open arms. In the distance, several Indian animals are visible among trees and low hills. The child smiles, showing that India is a country where many animals live.

pages.text: I am from India. I wave my beautiful green tail.
pages.brief: A peacock stands in a sunny garden, its long green tail feathers fanned out in a shimmering display. The bird turns its head as it waves its beautiful green tail. Lush plants and soft grass surround it.

pages.text: I am from India. You may spot my dark face as I leap from tree to tree.
pages.brief: A dark-faced langur monkey leaps from one tree branch to another in a dense forest. Its long tail trails behind as it jumps, and its dark face is clearly visible. Green leaves and branches fill the scene.

pages.text: I am from India. I have a wide head that looks like a hood.
pages.brief: A cobra rises from the grass, its wide head flattened into a hood. The snake's body curves on the ground, and its hood spreads wide. Sunlight filters through nearby plants and low bushes.

pages.text: I am from India. I am as big as a house, and I love to play in water.
pages.brief: A large elephant stands in a shallow river, spraying water over its back with its trunk. The elephant is huge, as big as a house, and it plays happily in the water. Muddy banks and green trees line the river.

pages.text: I am from India. I have orange and black stripes, and I move silently through the forest.
pages.brief: A tiger with orange and black stripes moves silently through a forest. Its body is low, paws quiet on the leaf-covered ground, and its eyes scan ahead. Tall trees and dappled light surround it.

pages.text: I am from India. My long, thin snout has a bump on the end.
pages.brief: A gharial crocodile rests on a sandy riverbank, its long, thin snout stretched out. A bump sits at the end of its snout. The river flows nearby, and reeds grow along the bank.

pages.text: I am from India. I am small but brave and famous for hunting snakes.
pages.brief: A small mongoose stands alert on a rock, its body low and brave. It faces a snake nearby, ready to hunt. Dry grass and stones surround the mongoose in a sunny clearing.

pages.text: I am from India. My thick, shaggy coat protects me in the cold mountains.
pages.brief: A shaggy yak stands on a cold mountain slope, its thick coat blowing in the wind. Snowy peaks rise behind it, and the yak's long hair covers its body. Rocks and patches of snow dot the ground.

pages.text: All of these animals are from India, and I am from India, too.
pages.brief: The young Indian child stands with a peacock, a langur, a cobra, an elephant, a tiger, a gharial, a mongoose and a yak gathered around. They all stand together in a sunny Indian landscape, showing they are all from India.

books.title: Some Birds Go
books.art_why: The book shows real birds and real migration, which can be photographed.

pages.text: Up in the sky, birds fly by. Where are the birds going?
pages.brief: Several birds fly across a wide open sky, wings spread, moving past one another as they travel. The sky fills the scene, and the birds are high above the ground. No destination is shown; they simply move onward together.

pages.text: Some birds migrate to other places for part of the year. Many migrate before winter in order to survive.
pages.brief: A group of birds flies away from a cold outdoor place toward another place, traveling before winter. Some birds stay behind as the others move across the pale sky. The scene shows birds migrating in order to survive.

pages.text: This bird migrates for fruit in winter. It returns for worms and insects in spring.
pages.brief: A bird flies from a winter tree holding fruit toward a spring scene where worms and insects lie on the ground. The bird returns with the change of season to find different food. Its wings are spread as it travels between the two places.

pages.text: This bird migrates in a V-shaped flock.
pages.brief: A flock of birds flies in a clear V shape high in the sky, each bird spaced behind the leaders. The formation stretches across the open air as the birds travel together. Wings are spread, and the group moves as one.

pages.text: This bird migrates at night and rests during the day.
pages.brief: At night, a group of birds flies through a dark sky. In daylight, the birds are settled and still, resting with wings tucked, outdoors under the sun. The same birds are shown flying by night and resting by day.

pages.text: This bird migrates when the air grows too cold.
pages.brief: A bird flies away through cold air, wings out, leaving a frosty outdoor place. The air looks chilly, and the bird is in motion, traveling onward. It moves across the sky when the cold becomes too much.

pages.text: This bird often migrates alone.
pages.brief: One bird flies by itself across an open sky, with no other birds nearby. Its wings are spread, and it travels alone above the land. The bird is the only one in the whole scene.

pages.text: This bird migrates in a flock of thousands.
pages.brief: A huge flock of birds fills the sky, with thousands of wings and bodies close together as they fly. The birds stretch across the view, moving as one enormous group. They crowd the air from side to side.

pages.text: This bird migrates across the water without stopping.
pages.brief: A bird flies low over open water, wings beating, with no land in sight. It keeps going straight across the water without landing or resting. The wide water stretches out below and ahead of the bird.

pages.text: Some birds fly down a mountain to migrate. Some birds fly thousands of miles to migrate. Wherever these birds go, they’ll always come back.
pages.brief: One bird flies down a mountain slope, while another travels a vast distance across land and sky. In the end, birds are shown returning to the same outdoor place they came from. Their journeys are long, but the birds come back.

books.title: Sleds
books.art_why: Sleds, snow, dogs, and riders are real subjects that can be photographed today.

pages.text: Who Sleds? Sometimes snow makes travel tricky. Sometimes people use sleds to travel on snow.
pages.brief: A snowy path or road where snow has made travel tricky. People are using sleds to move across the snow, with one person seated on a sled and another helping guide or pull it through the winter landscape.

pages.text: Some people use sleds for fun. Some people use sleds for sports. Some people use sleds for work.
pages.brief: Three kinds of sled use are shown: people riding sleds for fun, people taking part in sled sports, and people using sleds to help with work. The scenes show different sleds and riders in snowy outdoor settings.

pages.text: Fun Sleds This sled is long and wooden. It glides quickly on the snow.
pages.brief: A long wooden sled rests on or glides across snow. Its long runners and wooden body are visible as it moves quickly over the snowy ground, with no other kind of sled shown in the scene.

pages.text: This sled is filled with air. Spinning down a hill is fun.
pages.brief: A sled filled with air, like an inflatable snow tube, is shown on a snowy hill. It is spinning down the slope, with the rounded air-filled shape clearly visible as it slides over the snow.

pages.text: Sport Sleds This sled holds four people. Riders steer around sharp bends.
pages.brief: A sport sled carrying four people is shown on a snowy course. The riders are steering together around a sharp bend, leaning into the turn as the sled follows the curved path through the snow.

pages.text: This sled zips down an icy track. The rider goes head first.
pages.brief: A sled zips down an icy track. The rider lies head first on the sled, moving fast along the smooth ice, with the track stretching ahead and snow or ice around the racing path.

pages.text: Work Sleds This sled helps carry things. Dog teams sometimes race over the snow.
pages.brief: A work sled is shown helping carry things over the snow. A team of dogs races across the snowy ground, pulling the loaded sled behind them as they travel together quickly through the winter landscape.

pages.text: This sled has a rope. You can pull people or things on top.
pages.brief: A sled with a rope is shown on the snow. A person holds or pulls the rope, moving people or things placed on top of the sled across the snowy ground in a simple winter scene.

pages.text: Many Sleds Sleds and snow just go together. They help make winter fun.
pages.brief: Sleds are shown together with snow in a winter scene. Different sleds rest or move on the snowy ground, showing that sleds and snow go together and help make winter fun for the people using them.

books.title: Animal Dads
books.art_why: Real animals and their caring behaviors can be photographed today.

pages.text: Some animal dads don’t help much. These dads don’t help at all!
pages.brief: Two animal dads are shown nearby, not helping at all. They stand apart and do nothing to care for their young. The picture focuses on these dads that do not help much with their babies.

pages.text: Other animal dads are great! Which animal dads are those?
pages.brief: Several animal dads are shown in different places, looking after their young. One dad stands close to his babies, while others are pictured with their offspring nearby. The scene asks which animal dads are great helpers.

pages.text: This dad guards and cares for his chicks. He helps them all by himself for almost two years.
pages.brief: An animal dad stands guard beside his chicks. He stays close and cares for them by himself. The chicks are gathered near him in their habitat. The scene shows the dad helping his chicks alone and protecting them.

pages.text: This dad cleans bugs from his babies’ fur. He helps feed them. He carries them, too.
pages.brief: An animal dad picks bugs from his babies' fur. He cleans them and helps feed them. He also carries the babies with him. The babies stay close to the dad as he cares for them in their habitat.

pages.text: This dad holds eggs in his mouth. He helps them stay safe until they are born.
pages.brief: An animal dad holds eggs in his mouth. He keeps the eggs safe inside his mouth until they are born. The dad is shown with his mouth full of eggs, caring for them in this way.

pages.text: This dad eats food and spits it back up. Then he feeds it to his pups. Yum! He helps his pups grow strong.
pages.brief: An animal dad eats food and then spits it back up. He feeds the spit-up food to his pups. The pups gather near the dad as they eat. The dad helps his pups grow strong by feeding them this way.

pages.text: This dad carries tadpoles on his back. He helps them reach water.
pages.brief: An animal dad carries tadpoles on his back. The tiny tadpoles cling to him as he moves. He is helping them reach water. The scene shows the dad transporting the tadpoles on his back toward the water.

pages.text: This dad holds an egg on his feet. He helps keep it warm in the cold.
pages.brief: An animal dad holds a single egg on his feet. He stands in a cold, snowy place. The dad keeps the egg warm on his feet in the cold. The scene shows him carefully balancing the egg as he cares for it.

pages.text: This dad holds thousands of eggs in his pouch. He helps them grow and hatch.
pages.brief: An animal dad holds thousands of eggs in his pouch. The eggs are gathered inside the pouch on his body. He helps the eggs grow and hatch there. The scene shows the dad carrying the many eggs in his pouch.

pages.text: These dads help out with their young, too!
pages.brief: Several animal dads are shown with their young. Each dad stays close and helps out with his babies. The young are gathered near the dads in different places. The scene shows that these dads help care for their young, too.

books.title: Hibernation
books.art_why: Hibernating animals like bears, bats and frogs exist today, so real photographs are possible.

pages.text: No Food in Winter Some animals can’t find food in the winter. Some of these animals hibernate.
pages.brief: A snowy winter woodland with deep snow covering the bare ground. A few small wild animals stand among the trees, noses down, searching the frozen ground for something to eat. No food is visible anywhere, and the animals look around a cold, empty landscape.

pages.text: What Is Hibernating? Hibernating is like a deep sleep. This sleep can last for weeks.
pages.brief: A small furry animal curled tight into a ball, eyes closed, deep in sleep inside a snug underground burrow lined with dry leaves. Its body is tucked in, still and peaceful, showing the long deep sleep that can last for weeks.

pages.text: Animals breathe slowly when they hibernate. Their hearts beat slower. They do not eat.
pages.brief: Close view of a small hibernating animal asleep in its burrow, body curled and motionless in the dim earth-walled space. Its chest barely rises with slow, shallow breathing, and it lies still with no food nearby, quiet and peaceful.

pages.text: How Do They Stay Alive? Hibernating animals eat lots of food before winter. The food stays in their bodies as fat.
pages.brief: An autumn woodland with fallen leaves on the ground. A small animal sits up eating berries and nuts, cheeks full, gathering as much food as it can. Its body looks round and plump, storing food as fat before the cold winter arrives.

pages.text: Animals live off this fat while they sleep. They also need a safe place to sleep.
pages.brief: A sleeping animal curled inside a safe, dry den under a tree root, its body padded with fat, living off that stored fat while it sleeps. The den is snug and hidden, sheltered from the weather, a quiet safe place to rest.

pages.text: They need to be safe from the cold. They need to be safe from hungry animals.
pages.brief: Cutaway view of a deep burrow under the snow, a small hibernating animal asleep inside, warm and hidden. Above ground, snow covers the entrance, and a hungry wild animal noses at the frozen ground outside, unable to reach the sleeper.

pages.text: Hibernating Animals Some snakes and frogs hibernate. Some turtles and mice hibernate. Some squirrels and bats hibernate.
pages.brief: A group of hibernating animals in their winter resting places: a snake coiled in a rock crevice, a frog and a turtle in the mud, a mouse in a burrow, a squirrel curled in a leaf nest, and a bat hanging upside down in a cave.

pages.text: Some bears hibernate. Some raccoons and skunks hibernate, too. All the hibernating animals wake up in the spring.
pages.brief: A bear asleep in a den, a raccoon curled in a hollow tree and a skunk in a burrow. Around them, spring sunshine melts the snow, green shoots push up, and the animals begin to stir and wake up.

books.title: At the Airport
books.art_why: Airports exist today, so real photographs fit.

pages.text: What happens at the airport?
pages.brief: The airport is shown as a broad setting for the question of what happens there. The view presents the airport building as a large place, with no single activity singled out, so the scene simply introduces the airport itself.

pages.text: Travelers park their cars in big parking lots at the airport.
pages.brief: Travelers park their cars in a big parking lot at the airport. Several cars are parked in rows across the wide lot, and travelers are shown leaving their cars there before going into the airport.

pages.text: Travelers take buses to go to the main building at the airport.
pages.brief: Travelers take buses to go to the main building at the airport. A bus is shown carrying travelers toward the airport's main building, with travelers inside as they ride along to reach the main building.

pages.text: Travelers stand in line to check in with their airline at the airport.
pages.brief: Travelers stand in line to check in with their airline at the airport. A line of travelers is shown at an airline check-in counter, with travelers waiting their turn and facing staff at the counter.

pages.text: Travelers hand over their large bags at the airport.
pages.brief: Travelers hand over their large bags at the airport. A traveler is shown handing a large bag to a person at the airport, with the large bag passing from the traveler's hands to the other person.

pages.text: Travelers are searched to keep everyone safe at the airport.
pages.brief: Travelers are shown being searched at the airport, with the search taking place to keep everyone safe. The scene focuses on the travelers as they are searched, showing the search as the main action at the airport.

pages.text: Travelers ride on moving sidewalks to get around faster at the airport.
pages.brief: Travelers are shown riding on a moving sidewalk, standing on the moving surface as it carries them along so they can get around faster at the airport. The moving sidewalk is inside the airport, and travelers use it to move from place to place.

pages.text: Travelers buy food and magazines before their flights at the airport.
pages.brief: Travelers are shown at a shop or stand buying food and magazines, with the food and magazines displayed for them before their flights at the airport. The travelers look at the food and magazines and make their purchases before their flights.

pages.text: Travelers wait to get on their planes at the airport.
pages.brief: Travelers are shown waiting in a seating area near the planes, sitting or standing as they wait for their turn to get on their planes at the airport. The waiting travelers stay in the airport until it is time to board.

pages.text: Travelers get on their planes and fly away at the airport.
pages.brief: Travelers are shown getting on their planes and then flying away, with the planes lifting off from the airport as the travelers leave. The scene shows the travelers boarding their planes at the airport and the planes taking off into the sky.

books.title: Tunnels
books.art_why: Real tunnels, people and machines exist and can be photographed.

pages.text: Tunnels are long, narrow, covered passages. People use many kinds of tunnels.
pages.brief: A wide view outside several different tunnel entrances: a road tunnel, a train tunnel and a footpath tunnel. People walk, cycle and drive toward the openings. The tunnels are long, narrow, covered passages, and each one is used by people going about their day.

pages.text: Some tunnels go underground. They help people avoid traffic.
pages.brief: Inside an underground road tunnel, cars and a bus drive in two directions. The tunnel is beneath a busy city street, and the vehicles stay underground instead of waiting in traffic above. Lights line the curved walls, and the road stretches ahead.

pages.text: Some tunnels go underwater. They help people avoid taking boats.
pages.brief: A cross-section view of an underwater tunnel with cars driving through a thick tube. Above the tunnel is water, with a boat floating on the surface. The cars travel straight through the tunnel instead of taking a boat across the water.

pages.text: Some tunnels go through mountains. They help people avoid going around or over mountains.
pages.brief: A road tunnel cuts through a tall mountain. Cars and a truck drive into the dark entrance and come out the other side. The mountain rises high above, and the road goes straight through it instead of climbing around or over the peak.

pages.text: Some tunnels go under roads. They help people walk and bike safely.
pages.brief: A pedestrian and bicycle tunnel passes under a wide road. Children walk and adults ride bikes through the safe, separate passage while cars travel on the road above. The tunnel lets people cross without mixing with traffic.

pages.text: Some tunnels go deep into the Earth. They help people get rocks and metals.
pages.brief: Deep underground, miners work in a tunnel carved into rock. Their helmet lamps light rough walls with shiny metal veins. One miner uses a pick to break rocks free, while another carries a heavy sack of rocks. The tunnel goes deep into the Earth.

pages.text: Some tunnels have pipes. They help people get water.
pages.brief: A tunnel contains several large pipes running along its walls. Workers check the pipes, and clear water flows through them. The tunnel and pipes carry water from one place to another, helping people get the water they need.

pages.text: Some tunnels are slides. They help people have fun.
pages.brief: Children slide down a long, twisting tunnel slide at a playground. They laugh as they come out the bottom, and others wait their turn at the top. The slide is a tunnel that helps people have fun.

pages.text: Some tunnels are hidden. They help people travel in secret.
pages.brief: A hidden tunnel entrance is concealed in a hillside. Two people move quietly through the dark passage with a lantern, keeping out of sight. The tunnel is secret, and it lets people travel without being seen.

pages.text: Tunnels help people and things move from place to place.
pages.brief: A busy scene shows people and things moving through different tunnels: cars in a road tunnel, a train in a rail tunnel, a bike in a path tunnel and water in a pipe tunnel. All the tunnels help people and things move from place to place.

books.title: The Food Chain
books.art_why: Real plants and animals in a food chain can be shown in photographs.

pages.text: All plants need food in order to live. Green plants make food. They need air, water, and sunlight to make food. Most plants need soil, too. All animals need food in order to live. These animals eat plants. They are called plant eaters.
pages.brief: In a sunlit outdoor scene, green plants stand in soil with water and sunlight around them. Nearby, several animals nibble on plant leaves and stems, showing plant eaters feeding on plants.

pages.text: These animals eat other animals. They are called meat eaters. Plant eaters and meat eaters are part of a food chain. Most food chains begin with plants. The plants make food, which animals eat. Let’s look at a food chain.
pages.brief: A meat-eating animal catches and eats another animal. Beside it, a plant-eating animal stands near green plants. Together they show plant eaters and meat eaters as parts of a food chain that begins with plants.

pages.text: A grasshopper eats the leaves of a plant. The grasshopper grows bigger. A frog eats the grasshopper. The frog grows bigger. A fish eats the frog. The fish grows bigger.
pages.brief: A grasshopper chews the leaves of a green plant, growing bigger. A frog nearby catches and eats the grasshopper, growing bigger. Then a fish catches and eats the frog, growing bigger. The sequence shows one animal eating the next.

pages.text: A small bear catches the fish. The bear eats the fish. The bear grows bigger. This food chain has five parts. The green plant is the first part. The grasshopper is the second part. What are the other parts?
pages.brief: A small bear catches a fish and eats it, growing bigger. Green plants and a grasshopper are visible as earlier parts of the same five-part food chain. The scene shows the bear with its fish catch, completing the chain shown so far.

books.title: Seashells
books.art_why: Seashells and mollusks are real ocean subjects that can be photographed.

pages.text: Some animals grow bones inside their body. These bones are called a skeleton.
pages.brief: Inside the body of an animal, a skeleton of bones is shown in place, making clear that some animals grow bones within their bodies. The bones support the animal from the inside, and the surrounding body shape is visible around them.

pages.text: Some animals grow bones outside their body. These bones are called shells.
pages.brief: An animal is shown with a hard shell covering the outside of its body, like bones grown on the outside. The shell wraps around the body, making clear that some animals grow bones outside themselves.

pages.text: Some animals that live in the ocean grow seashells. These animals are called mollusks.
pages.brief: In the ocean, mollusks are shown with seashells growing on the outside of their soft bodies. They live in the water, and their seashells are part of them as ocean animals that grow seashells around themselves.

pages.text: Mollusks are soft, but their seashells are hard, like bones. Seashells protect mollusks from other animals. Seashells are also homes for mollusks.
pages.brief: A soft mollusk is tucked inside a hard seashell, safe from other animals nearby. The hard shell surrounds the soft body and acts as a home, showing how seashells protect mollusks and give them shelter.

pages.text: This mollusk lives in a seashell. Its seashell is bumpy.
pages.brief: A mollusk is shown living inside its seashell in the ocean. The shell has a bumpy surface all over it, and the soft mollusk stays within the hard, bumpy shell as its safe home.

pages.text: This mollusk lives in a seashell. Its seashell is striped.
pages.brief: A mollusk is shown living inside its seashell in the ocean water. The shell has stripes running across its surface all over it, and the soft mollusk stays within the hard, striped shell as its safe home.

pages.text: This mollusk lives in a seashell. Its seashell is spotted.
pages.brief: A mollusk is shown living inside its seashell in the ocean water. The shell has round spots all over its surface, and the soft mollusk stays within the hard, spotted shell as its safe home.

pages.text: This mollusk lives in a seashell. Its seashell is very large.
pages.brief: A mollusk is shown living inside a seashell that is very large. The huge shell surrounds the small soft mollusk, and the mollusk stays safely inside this big hard home in the blue ocean water.

pages.text: When mollusks die, they leave their shells behind.
pages.brief: Empty seashells are shown left behind after mollusks die. The soft mollusks are gone, and only their hard shells remain on the ocean floor in the water, lying still and empty where the mollusks once lived.

pages.text: Now other animals may live in seashells that mollusks have left behind.
pages.brief: Other animals are shown living inside seashells that mollusks have left behind. These animals shelter within the empty hard shells on the ocean floor, using the leftover seashells as homes after the mollusks are gone.

books.title: Are You From Brazil?
books.art_why: The book shows real Brazilian animals that can be photographed today.

pages.text: Brazil is my home. Many animals live here, too.
pages.brief: A wide green Brazilian rainforest with tall trees, broad leaves and a river winding through it. Several different animals are partly visible among the branches and near the water, showing that many animals make their home in Brazil. Warm sunlight filters through the canopy.

pages.text: Brazil is my home. I look like a red fox with long legs. A hairy mane rises along my back.
pages.brief: A tall, red-fox-like animal with very long legs stands in a grassy Brazilian clearing. A strip of shaggy hair rises along its back. Its ears are large and upright, and it looks across the open ground toward low bushes.

pages.text: Brazil is my home. My long tongue grabs insects to eat.
pages.brief: A long-snouted animal stands near a mound of earth in Brazil. Its narrow tongue stretches out to catch insects in the air. Its bushy tail sweeps behind it, and dry grass and soil surround its feet.

pages.text: Brazil is my home. I am the largest rodent in the world.
pages.brief: A large, sturdy rodent with a blunt face and small ears sits beside a Brazilian river. Its heavy body rests on short legs near muddy banks and thick green plants. Water and low vegetation fill the background.

pages.text: Brazil is my home. My skin is many pretty colors, but don’t touch me. I can kill with my poison.
pages.brief: A tiny, brightly colored frog clings to a wet green leaf in a Brazilian rainforest. Its skin shows several vivid colors. Raindrops sit on the leaf, and dark wet leaves and stems surround it in the shadows.

pages.text: Brazil is my home. I am a small monkey with a long tail.
pages.brief: A small monkey with a very long tail hangs from a thin branch in a Brazilian forest. Its tail curls down below it, and its hands grip the wood. Green leaves and vines fill the warm, humid background.

pages.text: Brazil is my home. I am the heaviest snake in the world.
pages.brief: A huge, thick snake lies coiled on muddy ground beside a Brazilian river. Its heavy body is patterned and broad, resting among wet grasses and low plants. The water and dense green forest edge sit behind it.

pages.text: Brazil is my home. I am very colorful with my long bill. Some people keep me as a pet.
pages.brief: A brightly colored bird with a very long, large bill perches on a branch in Brazil. Its feathers show strong colors, and its bill points forward. Green leaves and soft light fill the rainforest around it.

pages.text: Brazil is my home. Watch out if you swim in the river. My teeth are sharp!
pages.brief: A sharp-toothed fish swims in a Brazilian river, its mouth open to show pointed teeth. Murky green water surrounds it, with dark plants and soft ripples. The fish's eye and fin are visible as it moves.

pages.text: All these animals are from Brazil. I am from Brazil, too!
pages.brief: A wide Brazilian landscape brings together the animals from the book: the red-fox-like animal, the long-tongued insect eater, the large rodent, the colorful frog, the small long-tailed monkey, the huge snake, the long-billed bird and the sharp-toothed fish, each in forest, grass or river water.

books.title: At the Watering Hole
books.art_why: The book shows real savanna animals at a real watering hole, so photographs fit.

pages.text: At the Watering Hole.
pages.brief: A wide, quiet view of a watering hole. Still water fills a low basin in open ground, with dry earth around the edge. The scene is empty and calm, showing only the place where animals will come to drink.

pages.text: It is the dry season on the African savanna. Animals come to the watering hole to drink.
pages.brief: On the dry African savanna, a watering hole sits under a wide sky. Several animals gather at the water's edge and lower their heads to drink. The ground around them looks dry, and the animals are arriving from the open land.

pages.text: Some animals come alone to drink. A small bird bows to take a drink.
pages.brief: A small bird stands alone at the edge of the watering hole. It bows its head down toward the water to take a drink. No other animals are close by, and the bird is by itself in the open setting.

pages.text: A tall giraffe bends to take a drink.
pages.brief: A tall giraffe stands at the watering hole and bends its long neck down low. It stretches toward the water to take a drink. The giraffe is shown beside the water, with its legs planted on the ground.

pages.text: A big hippo dives to take a drink.
pages.brief: A big hippo is at the watering hole and dives down into the water to take a drink. Its large body is partly in the water, and the hippo is shown in the act of diving near the edge.

pages.text: A heavy rhino stops to take a drink.
pages.brief: A heavy rhino stands at the watering hole and stops at the water's edge to take a drink. Its strong body and horn are visible as it pauses by the water. The rhino is alone in the open scene.

pages.text: Some animals come together to drink. A flock of storks comes to take a drink.
pages.brief: A flock of storks comes together at the watering hole to take a drink. Many storks stand close to one another at the water's edge, with their heads lowered toward the water. They gather as a group in the open setting.

pages.text: A parade of elephants comes to take a drink.
pages.brief: A parade of elephants comes to the watering hole to take a drink. The elephants move in a line toward the water, with their large bodies and trunks visible. They are grouped together as they arrive at the edge.

pages.text: A pack of dogs comes to take a drink.
pages.brief: A pack of dogs comes to the watering hole to take a drink. The dogs gather close together at the water's edge, with their heads toward the water. They are shown as a pack in the open setting near the watering hole.

pages.text: A herd of zebras comes to take a drink.
pages.brief: A herd of zebras comes to the watering hole to take a drink. Many zebras stand together at the water's edge, with their striped bodies visible. They gather as a herd, lowering their heads toward the water to drink.

pages.text: Some animals come to drink and hunt. Lions, leopards, and hyenas look for a meal.
pages.brief: Lions, leopards, and hyenas are at the watering hole, looking for a meal. The predators watch from around the water as animals come to drink and hunt. Their eyes and bodies show them searching for food in the open setting.

books.title: Hatching Eggs
books.art_why: Every subject here is real today — eggs, chicks, an incubator, a classroom, a sink and a coop — so real photographs work.

pages.text: Hatching Eggs i.
pages.brief: A close, softly lit view of a small group of pale brown chicken eggs resting together on clean bedding. The eggs sit still and whole, filling the frame, waiting for what comes next.

pages.text: Chicks are baby chickens. Chicks hatch from eggs.
pages.brief: A fluffy yellow chick stands beside a cracked-open eggshell on a soft surface, tiny wings held close to its body. Next to it sits another whole egg. The chick turns its head toward the shell pieces.

pages.text: You can hatch chicks at school.
pages.brief: In a bright classroom, several children stand around a table watching a small clear-topped incubator. A teacher leans in beside them, pointing toward the eggs inside. Desks and shelves fill the background.

pages.text: First, wash your hands. This helps you and the eggs stay clean.
pages.brief: A child's hands are held under a running tap at a school sink, soap lather on the fingers and wrists. Water splashes into the white basin, and folded paper towels wait on the counter beside it.

pages.text: Next, mark the eggs with an X and an O. This helps you tell one side from the other.
pages.brief: Two hands hold a brown egg steady while a marker draws a clear X on the shell. Nearby on the table, other eggs already marked with an X and an O sit in a card tray.

pages.text: Then, put the eggs inside an incubator. This helps the eggs stay warm.
pages.brief: A pair of hands lowers an egg carefully through the open lid of an incubator, setting it gently on the rack inside. The clear-topped incubator sits on a classroom table, softly lit.

pages.text: Next, put water inside the incubator. This keeps the eggs from getting dry.
pages.brief: A hand tips a small cup of water into the narrow channel inside the incubator, beside the eggs. Droplets glisten in the groove while the eggs stay dry on their rack above.

pages.text: Each day, turn the eggs three times. This helps the growing chicks move around.
pages.brief: A hand reaches into the incubator and gently rolls one egg over on the rack, turning it. The other eggs wait nearby. Behind them, a classroom shelf and window show softly out of focus.

pages.text: In about three weeks, check the eggs for cracks. Finally, the chicks will hatch over the next day or two!
pages.brief: A close view of the eggs after weeks of waiting: fine cracks spread across one shell as the first hole opens, and the tip of a small beak shows at another egg beside it.

pages.text: Wait one more day before you touch the chicks. Then, feed the chicks.
pages.brief: A child crouches beside a shallow dish and sprinkles chick feed while two small fluffy chicks peck at it. Their tiny bodies crowd close to the dish on a clean floor.

pages.text: Last, find them a good home.
pages.brief: A small group of young chickens scratches in the straw of a wooden coop in a sunny garden. A feeder and water dish sit nearby, and green grass shows beyond the open coop door.

books.title: Cascarones
books.art_why: Cascarones are real painted eggshells made and used today.

pages.text: Cascarones are painted eggshells. Cascarones help people celebrate in Mexico and the United States. Word Wise.
pages.brief: A bright tabletop scene shows a bowl of painted eggshells in many colours — red, yellow, blue and green — with confetti spilling from a few. In the background, families in Mexico and the United States celebrate together outdoors with festive decorations and smiles.

pages.text: Cascarones are fun to make. Poke a hole in an eggshell.
pages.brief: A child's hands hold a plain white eggshell over a table. One finger presses a small hole into the top of the shell, with tiny cracks spreading. A bowl of whole eggs sits nearby.

pages.text: Cascarones are fun to make. Take the egg out of the shell.
pages.brief: The same child gently blows through the hole in the eggshell, and the raw egg slides out into a small glass bowl below. The empty shell rests in the child's other hand on a kitchen table.

pages.text: Cascarones are fun to make. Fill the egg with confetti.
pages.brief: The child uses a small spoon to fill the empty eggshell with bright confetti, colours spilling onto a bright kitchen table. A jar of confetti sits open beside a small bowl, and the shell is nearly full.

pages.text: Cascarones are painted many ways. Cascarones make people laugh.
pages.brief: A group of children and adults sit around a table, laughing as they paint eggshells in many different colours and patterns. Brushes and pots of paint are scattered across the table, and finished cascarones rest in a basket.

pages.text: Some cascarones are painted with faces. Cascarones make people laugh.
pages.brief: A close view of several cascarones on a table, each painted with a different smiling face — round eyes, curved mouths and rosy cheeks. A child's hands hold one up, and nearby friends laugh at the funny faces.

pages.text: Some cascarones are painted with animals. Cascarones make people laugh.
pages.brief: Cascarones on a table are painted with animals: a cat, a dog, a bird and a fish, each in bright colours. A child points at one, and a small group of friends giggles together around the table.

pages.text: Some cascarones are painted with fruits. Cascarones make people laugh.
pages.brief: A row of cascarones shows painted fruits — a red apple, a yellow banana, a green pear and a purple grape cluster. Children lean in to look, laughing, with paint pots and brushes on the table beside them.

pages.text: People crack cascarones over their friends’ heads.
pages.brief: Outdoors in a sunny park, a child gently cracks a cascarone over a friend's head, and bright confetti spills into the friend's hair. The friend laughs and others nearby watch with big smiles, ready for their turn.

pages.text: People say cascarones bring good luck!
pages.brief: Children and adults celebrate together in a sunny park, holding cracked cascarones with confetti in their hair. They smile and cheer, believing the shells bring good luck, with colourful streamers, flowers and happy faces all around.

books.title: The Bald Eagle
books.art_why: Real bald eagles, coins, flags and buildings exist today.

pages.text: The bald eagle is a symbol of the United States.
pages.brief: A bald eagle stands in profile with a white head, dark brown body, and hooked yellow beak, shown in a clear outdoor nature view; the bird looks alert as the national symbol of the United States.

pages.text: The United States has many symbols. A symbol is something that stands for something else.
pages.brief: A bald eagle appears among a group of recognizable American symbols in a clear, simple arrangement, showing that the United States has many symbols and that each one stands for something else in the nation.

pages.text: The bald eagle is strong. It stands for the strength of the United States.
pages.brief: A bald eagle spreads its large wings and grips a sturdy perch with strong talons, its white head and dark body held upright in an open outdoor view; the powerful pose stands for the strength of the United States.

pages.text: The bald eagle is beautiful. It stands for the beauty of the United States.
pages.brief: A bald eagle is shown in a close, clear view in soft natural light, its white head and dark feathers neat and striking; the bird’s beautiful appearance stands for the beauty of the United States.

pages.text: The bald eagle is free. It stands for the freedom of the United States.
pages.brief: A bald eagle flies high with wide wings fully open against an open sky, moving freely over a broad natural landscape in a clear view; the eagle’s free flight stands for the freedom of the United States.

pages.text: The bald eagle is on money in the United States. It is on many coins.
pages.brief: A bald eagle is shown on United States money, with several coins spread out in a neat arrangement so the eagle design is easy to see; the coins rest on a plain surface in a clear close view.

pages.text: The bald eagle is on flags in the United States. It is on many state flags.
pages.brief: A bald eagle appears on United States flags, including several state flags displayed upright in a clear row in a bright indoor setting; the eagle design is visible on each flag against a plain background.

pages.text: The bald eagle is on public buildings in the United States. It is on many city halls.
pages.brief: A bald eagle is shown on a public building in the United States, with a city hall entrance and stone facade clearly visible; the eagle design sits above the entrance as part of the building.

pages.text: The bald eagle is the national bird of the United States.
pages.brief: A bald eagle stands alert in a clear natural view, its white head and dark body fully visible with a calm, proud posture; the bird is shown as the national bird of the United States.

pages.text: The bald eagle is an important symbol of the United States.
pages.brief: A bald eagle is shown in a strong, clear view, its white head and dark wings held high as an important symbol in an open outdoor setting; the bird stands for the United States in a simple, respectful presentation.

books.title: Gaggle, Herd, and Pod
books.art_why: All the animals and people shown exist in the real world today, so real photographs fit.

pages.text: Animals are everywhere. Sometimes they gather in groups. Animal groups have different names.
pages.brief: A wide open landscape shows many kinds of animals spread across grass, sky and water, each kind standing together in its own small group. Some are on the ground, some in the air, some near the water, all gathered with others of their kind.

pages.text: A group of geese is a gaggle. A gaggle of geese stands together.
pages.brief: A gaggle of geese stands together on short green grass beside calm water. Their long necks are raised, bodies close in one loose cluster, feathers lit by soft daylight. A few face different directions while the group stays packed together in the open.

pages.text: A group of bats is a colony. A colony of bats may leave its cave all at once.
pages.brief: Deep inside a dark cave, a colony of bats clings to the rocky ceiling. At the cave mouth, hundreds of bats stream out into the dusk all at once, wings spread, filling the opening as they leave the cave together in a thick, flowing crowd.

pages.text: A murder is a group of crows. This murder gathers at sunset.
pages.brief: A murder of crows gathers in bare branches at sunset. The orange sky glows behind dark silhouettes of many crows perched close together, some with wings half open, others landing. They cluster across the branches, collecting in one noisy group as the light fades.

pages.text: A group of whales is a pod. A pod of whales swims together.
pages.brief: A pod of whales swims together through deep blue ocean water. Several large bodies glide side by side near the surface, backs breaking the water, fins and tails visible. They move in the same direction, close as a group, with light rippling across the waves above them.

pages.text: A smack is a group of jellyfish. A smack travels on ocean waves.
pages.brief: A smack of jellyfish drifts on ocean waves. Many soft, rounded bells float together near the surface, trailing tentacles down into green-blue water. Gentle swells lift them, and the whole group travels along with the moving water, packed loosely across the frame.

pages.text: A group of zebras is a herd. Sometimes a herd races together.
pages.brief: A herd of zebras races together across dry grassland. Striped bodies run shoulder to shoulder, legs stretched mid-stride, dust rising behind them. They charge in the same direction across the open plain, a tight moving group under bright daylight, manes and tails flying.

pages.text: A pack is a group of wolves. A pack works together to hunt.
pages.brief: A pack of wolves works together to hunt across a snowy landscape. Several wolves fan out through low brush and snow, heads low, moving as one group. Some push forward while others flank the sides, all focused in the same direction through the cold, pale light.

pages.text: A group of humans can be a family. A group of humans can be a neighborhood. What other groups do you know?
pages.brief: A family stands together outside their home, and beyond them a neighborhood spreads out with houses and people out on the street. Adults and children appear in both views, gathered in small groups, showing people together as families and as neighbors in a community.

books.title: Changing Seasons
books.art_why: Seasons and everyday weather are real, observable things today, so photographs fit.

pages.text: I live where the weather changes during the year. It changes with each season. We have four seasons. We start with spring. Then comes summer. Then comes fall. Then comes winter.
pages.brief: A child stands in the yard of a countryside home, looking out over fields and trees where the weather changes through the year. Around the same landscape, spring, summer, fall and winter follow one another in order.

pages.text: It is spring and the snow melts. It gets warmer, and plants begin to grow. The days get longer, and the nights get shorter. I wear my jacket. It is summer. It gets hot, and the plants grow bigger. The days are long, and the nights are short. I wear my shorts.
pages.brief: The same child in a jacket stands outside as spring snow melts into wet ground, the air warmer and small green plants pushing up. Then, in shorts, the child stands under tall leafy plants in hot summer sun, with a long bright day and a short dark night.

pages.text: It is fall. It gets cooler, and the plants stop growing. The days get shorter, and the nights get longer. I wear my sweater. It is winter. It is cold, and many plants die. The snow begins to fall, and the days are short. I wear my coat.
pages.brief: The child in a sweater stands among plants that have stopped growing as the air cools, in shorter daylight. Then, in a warm coat, the child stands in cold winter air while snow falls and many plants have died, the day short.

pages.text: The weather has changed with each season. It got warmer and warmer. The days got longer and longer. Then it got cooler and cooler. The days got shorter and shorter. Next, I will see spring again. The cycle will start all over.
pages.brief: The child watches the same land change again: warmth rising, days stretching longer, then cooling, days shrinking shorter. The landscape turns back toward spring, and the whole round of seasons begins again.

books.title: How Do They Move?
books.art_why: Real animals and their body parts can be photographed.

pages.text: Animals, animals, how do they move? These animals move on land. They have strong legs for hopping and jumping. Can you name them? Animals, animals, how do they move? These animals move on land. They have strong legs for running. Can you name them?
pages.brief: On land, a group of animals with strong legs is shown hopping and jumping. Nearby, another group of land animals with strong legs runs across open ground. The scene shows the different leg movements used for hopping, jumping and running.

pages.text: Animals, animals, how do they move? These animals move on land. They have many legs for crawling. Can you name them? Animals, animals, how do they move? These animals move on land. They have two legs for walking and running. Can you name them?
pages.brief: On land, many-legged animals crawl close to the ground, their legs moving in a ripple. In another part of the scene, two-legged animals walk and run upright on open ground, showing how legs support walking and running.

pages.text: Animals, animals, how do they move? These animals move in the air. They have wings for flying. Can you name them? Animals, animals, how do they move? These animals move in water. They have fins and flippers for swimming. Can you name them?
pages.brief: In the air, animals with wings fly above the ground. Below or beside them, animals with fins and flippers swim through water, their bodies adapted for moving in a watery habitat. The page contrasts flight above with swimming below.

pages.text: Animals, animals, how do they move? These animals move in the trees. They have long arms for swinging. Can you name them? Animals, animals, how do they move? These animals move on land. They have no legs, no arms, no wings, and no fins. Can you name them?
pages.brief: In the trees, long-armed animals swing from branches. On land, animals with no legs, no arms, no wings and no fins move along the ground, showing a very different way of moving without limbs or flight.

books.title: Needs and Wants
books.art_why: Everyday children, food, clothes and bikes are real-world subjects that suit photographs.

pages.text: We all need things. We need food, water, and air. We need a home and clothing, too. We all want things. We want things that make us happy. We want things that are fun.
pages.brief: A group of children outdoors in a sunny neighborhood stand together with a plate of food, a glass of water, and a warm house nearby; one child wears a warm coat, another breathes the fresh air, and one holds a fun toy.

pages.text: Erin needs water to drink. She wants a glass of lemonade. Jacob needs food to eat. He wants pasta for dinner.
pages.brief: Erin, a young girl, sits at a table holding a glass of water, with a pitcher of lemonade beside her; Jacob, a boy, sits at a dinner table with a plate of food and a bowl of pasta in front of him.

pages.text: Erin needs a warm coat for the winter. She wants a long red coat. Jacob needs air to breathe. He wants some wind to fly his kite.
pages.brief: Erin stands outdoors in winter, holding a warm coat and looking at a long red coat; nearby, Jacob stands in an open field breathing fresh air, holding a kite string as the wind lifts his kite behind him.

pages.text: Erin needs to stay safe from the storm. She wants to go under her bed. Jacob needs a way to get to school. He wants a new bike.
pages.brief: Rain and wind from a storm beat against the windows of a house; inside, Erin kneels beside her bed, looking underneath it. Outside, Jacob stands on a path near his school, looking at a new bike.

pages.text: Erin needs to read a book for school. She wants to read a funny book. What kinds of things do you want? Do you really need those things?
pages.brief: Erin sits at a table with a school book open in front of her and a funny book with a playful picture beside it; she smiles and looks thoughtful, resting her chin on her hand as she thinks about what she wants.

books.title: Glassblowing
books.art_why: Glassblowing is a real modern craft with real people, ovens and tools.

pages.text: I am a glassblower. Watch me make a beautiful glass bowl.
pages.brief: A glassblower stands at work holding a long pipe, focused on making a beautiful glass bowl. The person is the central figure, with hands on the pipe and a clear view of the glass at the end. The scene shows the glassblower actively creating the bowl.

pages.text: The oven that holds the glass is very, very hot. The hot glass is runny, like honey.
pages.brief: A very, very hot oven holds the glass inside, glowing brightly. The hot glass looks runny, like honey, and the glassblower is beside the oven. The heat is the focus as the soft glass waits to be shaped.

pages.text: I dip my long pipe into the hot glass. I roll the pipe on the table to smooth and cool the glass.
pages.brief: The glassblower dips a long pipe into the hot glass. Then the glassblower rolls the pipe on a table, smoothing and cooling the glass as it turns. The pipe and the soft glass are the main focus in this step.

pages.text: I blow into the pipe. I blow a bubble in the gooey glass. I try not to blow too hard.
pages.brief: The glassblower blows into the long pipe, making a bubble form in the gooey glass. The glassblower's face and hands show care, trying not to blow too hard. The bubble grows inside the soft, sticky glass at the end of the pipe.

pages.text: I add other colors to make the bowl even more beautiful.
pages.brief: The glassblower adds other colors to the glass bowl, making it even more beautiful. Small amounts of color meet the hot glass while the glassblower works carefully. The bowl begins to show bright, mixed colors as it is being made.

pages.text: I dip my pipe into the oven again. The oven makes the colors flow.
pages.brief: The glassblower dips the pipe into the oven again. Inside the very hot oven, the colors flow through the glass and blend. The glassblower watches the oven as the heat softens the colors and helps them move.

pages.text: My tools help me to shape the glass.
pages.brief: The glassblower uses tools to shape the glass. The tools press and guide the glass while the glassblower turns it carefully. The focus is on the hands, the tools, and the glass taking shape.

pages.text: I spin the glass as fast as I can. The bowl gets wider and wider.
pages.brief: The glassblower spins the glass on the pipe as fast as possible. The bowl turns round and round, getting wider and wider with the speed. The glassblower's hands stay steady as the spinning bowl grows.

pages.text: I break off the pipe. I heat the glass again to make it smooth.
pages.brief: The glassblower breaks the glass off the pipe. Then the glassblower heats the glass again at the oven, making it smooth. The bowl is handled carefully as the pipe comes away and the heat smooths the glass.

pages.text: The glass cools slowly. My beautiful bowl is done.
pages.brief: The beautiful glass bowl cools slowly after the work is done. The glassblower leaves it to cool, and the finished bowl stands ready. The bowl is smooth and complete, the result of all the careful steps.

books.title: Weird White House Pets
books.art_why: The book shows real animals, presidents and the White House, all of which can be photographed.

pages.text: Odd Pets Most presidents have had pets. They have had dogs, cats, birds, and horses. But some very odd pets have lived at the White House, too.
pages.brief: A view of the White House with several presidents standing on the lawn, surrounded by ordinary pets: dogs, cats, birds and horses. The animals are calm and varied, showing the common pets presidents have kept, while the building stands clearly in the background.

pages.text: Sheep lived at the White House. They kept the grass trimmed. Calvin Coolidge A raccoon lived at the White House. A president walked it on a leash.
pages.brief: On the White House lawn, a small flock of sheep grazes and trims the grass. Nearby, President Calvin Coolidge walks a raccoon on a leash along a garden path, with the White House standing behind them in the background.

pages.text: A snake lived at the White House. A president’s daughter took care of it. Goats lived at the White House. One pulled a president’s grandchildren in a cart.
pages.brief: Inside the White House, a president’s daughter gently cares for a snake. Outside on the grounds, goats pull a small cart carrying the president’s grandchildren, with the White House and lawn visible in the background.

pages.text: A flying squirrel lived at the White House. A president let it climb on him. Bears lived at the White House. A president walked them in the garden.
pages.brief: A flying squirrel climbs on a president inside the White House. In the garden outside, a president calmly walks two bears on leashes along a path, with trees and the White House visible behind them.

pages.text: An alligator lived at the White House. It lived in a bathtub. Pets That Couldn’t Stay Elephants, lions, a tiger, and a hippo were gifts to presidents. They went to live at a zoo.
pages.brief: Inside a White House bathroom, an alligator rests in a bathtub. At a zoo, elephants, a lion, a tiger and a hippo stand in separate outdoor enclosures, showing the large gift animals that could not stay at the White House.

books.title: In a Chinese Garden
books.art_why: A real Chinese garden exists today, so photographs can show it.

pages.text: In a Chinese Garden.
pages.brief: A quiet Chinese garden is shown in a wide, peaceful view. Soft greenery and a traditional garden setting fill the scene, inviting a visitor to come inside. The garden looks calm and ready to explore.

pages.text: I’m visiting a Chinese garden. I enter a gate without doors.
pages.brief: A young child visitor steps through a gate without doors into a Chinese garden. The child looks ahead into the garden, ready to explore. The open gate has no door panels, and the child crosses the entrance.

pages.text: I see a lot of water. It looks as smooth as a mirror. I can see things in it. I’m glad for water to drink.
pages.brief: A child visitor looks into still, mirror-smooth water in a Chinese garden. The child sees reflected things in the water and is glad the water is there to drink. The water surface is calm and reflective.

pages.text: I see a huge rock. The rock looks so strong. It will not move or fall down. I’m glad I’m strong now, too.
pages.brief: A child visitor stands before a huge rock in a Chinese garden. The rock looks strong and steady, set firmly in place so it will not move or fall. The child stands near it, feeling strong too.

pages.text: I see trees. They stand tall and give shade. I’m glad for trees to rest under on a sunny day.
pages.brief: Tall trees stand in the Chinese garden and spread shade. A child visitor rests beneath them on a sunny day, glad for the cool shade. The trees rise high above the child and the sunny garden around them.

pages.text: The Chinese garden is beautiful and peaceful. I’ll remember it whenever I see water, rocks, and trees.
pages.brief: A child visitor stands in the Chinese garden, taking in its beautiful and peaceful view. Water, rocks, and trees are around the garden. The child will remember this place whenever seeing water, rocks, and trees again.

pages.text: gate tree water.
pages.brief: A Chinese garden scene shows a gate, a tree, and water together. The gate stands open, the tree grows nearby, and water lies calm in the garden. These garden features are gathered in the scene.
